claims.claim: Tall wheat competes better for light but lodges (collapses) under the heavier grain produced with nitrogen fertilizer; Borlaug bred shorter, stronger stalks to prevent this.
claims.episode_span: Tall landraces had evolved under nutrient-poor conditions where extra height helped them compete for light, yet the same height became a liability once nitrogen supply rose.
claims.supporting_quote: Taller wheat grasses better compete for sunlight but tend to collapse under the weight of the extra grain—a trait called lodging—from the rapid growth spurts induced by nitrogen fertilizer Borlaug used in the poor soil.

claims.claim: In 1953 Borlaug acquired the Japanese dwarf wheat Norin 10 (bred by Gonjiro Inazuka in Iwate Prefecture) and used its short straw in his crosses.
claims.episode_span: The first concrete redesign step was to import the short, stiff straw of the Japanese Norin 10 variety, whose reduced height had already been noticed by U.S. Department of Agriculture observers.
claims.supporting_quote: In 1953, he acquired a Japanese dwarf variety of wheat called Norin 10 developed by the agronomist Gonjiro Inazuka in Iwate Prefecture

claims.claim: Borlaug's shuttle breeding advanced two wheat generations per year between two Mexican stations about 700 miles apart (the Yaqui Valley near Ciudad Obregon and the central highlands near Chapingo).
claims.episode_span: seed was advanced two generations per year by sending material from the mild winter environment of Ciudad Obregón in Sonora to the cooler, longer-day summer station at Chapingo or Toluca
claims.supporting_quote: As of 1945, wheat would then be bred at locations 700 miles (1,000 km) apart, 10 degrees apart in latitude, and 8,500 feet (2600 m) apart in altitude.

claims.claim: Semi-dwarf wheat (Norin 10/Brevor 14 derivatives) partitions a larger share of assimilate into grain, raising yield rather than total biomass.
claims.episode_span: the total above-ground biomass stayed roughly the same while the proportion allocated to grain rose sharply
claims.supporting_quote: Norin 10/Brevor 14 is semi-dwarf (one-half to two-thirds the height of standard varieties) and produces more stalks and thus more heads of grain per plant. Also, larger amounts of assimilate were partitioned into the actual grains, further increasing the yield.

claims.claim: Borlaug's Mexican dwarf varieties, when properly cultivated, had grain-yield potential roughly double or triple that of the best older varieties.
claims.episode_span: By the mid-1960s the best dwarf selections were delivering roughly two to three times the grain per hectare of the older tall varieties under the same irrigation and nitrogen regimes.
claims.source_title: Norman Borlaug - Nobel Lecture: The Green Revolution, Peace, and Humanity
claims.supporting_quote: permits these varieties, when properly cultivated, to express their high genetic grain-yield potential – in general, double or triple that of the best yielders among older

claims.claim: The dwarf varieties' yield advantage depended on reliable water and fertilizer; the breakthrough increases came in irrigated areas.
claims.episode_span: the new plant required reliable water and nitrogen to express its higher grain fraction; without those inputs the dwarf lines yielded no better than the old tall ones
claims.source_title: Norman Borlaug - Nobel Lecture: The Green Revolution, Peace, and Humanity
claims.supporting_quote: Moreover, it must be emphasized that thus far the great increase in production has been in irrigated areas.
